approach: The authors conduct a narrative literature review. They systematically organize existing knowledge into thematic sections: an overview of melanoma pathogenesis, mechanisms of ICIs, detailed roles of specific immune cell subsets, the composition and function of the skin TME (cellular, ECM, soluble factors, microbiome, metabolism), and clinical applications/challenges. The synthesis relies on citing established clinical trials (e.g., CheckMate, KEYNOTE series) and mechanistic studies from the literature to build a comprehensive picture of the field.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides a comprehensive synthesis of non-gut microbial influences (specifically skin microbiome) and physical/metabolic aspects of the TME on ICI efficacy in melanoma.
contribution_and_limits.limits: As a narrative review, it does not present new primary data. The focus is heavily skewed towards cutaneous melanoma, limiting direct applicability to other solid tumors or mucosal melanoma without further validation.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Highlights the interplay between skin-specific immune residents (TRM, LCs) and systemic ICI therapy.
contribution_and_limits.limits: Mechanistic links described are largely correlational or based on preclinical models; causal evidence in human patients is often inferred rather than directly demonstrated in this text.

key_findings.finding: High infiltration of CD8+ T cells and presence of tertiary lymphoid structures (B cells) are associated with better ICI response; conversely, high M2 macrophage infiltration and regulatory T cells correlate with resistance.
Skin-resident memory T cells (TRM) and Langerhans cells play critical roles in local immunity; their dysfunction or depletion contributes to immune evasion.

Increased extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness acts as a physical barrier to T cell infiltration, contributing to ICI resistance. Accumulation of immunosuppressive metabolites (lactate, kynurenine) inhibits immune cell function.
Higher diversity of the skin microbiome is associated with improved objective response rates to PD-1 inhibitors compared to low diversity.

Combination therapies (e.g., anti-PD-1 + anti-CTLA-4) show superior survival outcomes in metastatic melanoma but with higher toxicity; neoadjuvant approaches show promise for pathological complete responses.

problem_or_question: To address the complexity of ICI response and resistance in melanoma by synthesizing knowledge on how tumor-immune cell interactions and the specific skin microenvironment influence therapeutic outcomes, aiming to provide theoretical foundations for optimizing immunotherapy strategies.
research_scope: Melanoma (primarily cutaneous, with some mention of mucosal/acral subtypes), focusing on the mechanisms of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), interactions between various immune cells and the tumor microenvironment (TME), and clinical applications across different disease stages.
work_summary: This review article summarizes the current understanding of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy in melanoma. It details the mechanisms of action of ICIs targeting PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4, and comprehensively discusses the roles of diverse immune cells (T cells, NK cells, macrophages, T helper cells, dendritic cells, B cells) and specific components of the skin tumor microenvironment (including resident memory T cells, Langerhans cells, extracellular matrix, cytokines/chemokines, metabolites, and the skin microbiome). The paper also reviews the clinical efficacy of ICIs in metastatic, adjuvant, and neoadjuvant settings, addresses challenges such as resistance and immune-related adverse events, and outlines future research directions.
